bib.title: Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch), ch. 4: Implementing a GPT model from scratch to generate text

question: How do the layer norm, GELU feed-forward, shortcut connections and transformer block assemble into a GPT-2 small model that maps token IDs to next-token logits?
contributions: Placeholder DummyGPTModel, LayerNorm, GELU, FeedForward, shortcut demo, TransformerBlock, GPTModel, generate_text_simple
Parameter and memory counting for GPT-2 small, including the weight-tying discrepancy

results.claim: The GPT-2 small config used throughout has 50,257 vocab, 1,024 context, 768 emb, 12 heads, 12 layers, dropout 0.1, no QKV bias.
Built module by module with a separate output head and no weight tying, the model has 163,009,536 parameters, not 124M.
Removing the output head's parameters (weight tying) gives the GPT-2 small count of 124,412,160.
results.quote: Number of trainable parameters considering weight tying: 124,412,160

results.claim: The 163M-parameter model needs 621.83 MB in float32.
results.quote: Total size of the model: 621.83 MB

results.claim: Author reports that separate token-embedding and output layers gave better training and model performance than weight tying, so the implementation keeps them separate.
results.quote: ken embedding and output layers results in better training and model

results.claim: Without shortcut connections the mean absolute gradient shrinks from 0.00505 at layers.4 to 0.000202 at layers.0 (vanishing gradient).
results.setup: 5-layer GELU net, layer_sizes [3,3,3,3,3,1], input [1,0,-1], target 0, MSE loss, seed 123

results.claim: With shortcut connections layers.0 keeps a gradient of 0.2217 versus 1.3259 at layers.4.
An untrained GPT-2 small generates gibberish with greedy decoding ('Hello, I am Featureiman Byeswickattribute argue').
results.quote: Hello, I am Featureiman Byeswickattribute argue

results.claim: The feed-forward layer expands 768 to 3,072 (factor 4) and contracts back.
results.quote:
the inputs

results.claim: Pre-LayerNorm (norm before attention and FFN) is used; the original transformer's Post-LayerNorm often leads to worse training dynamics.
results.quote: known as Post-LayerNorm, which often leads to worse training dynamics.

limits: Chapter implements the architecture only; the model is untrained and outputs gibberish, training is in chapter 5.
Parameter-count discrepancy is explained by weight tying; the book keeps untied heads for training.
Gradient demo is one toy 5-layer net, one seed, one input.
Text says figure 4.18 where it means 4.8 (ReLU corner); text says weights loaded in chapter 6 (book's own numbering).
practices: Apply LayerNorm before attention and before the feed-forward layer (Pre-LayerNorm), with a shortcut around each (4.5).
Use GELU (tanh approximation, as GPT-2 did) in the feed-forward layer, expanding the hidden size 4x then contracting (4.3).
Use unbiased=False in LayerNorm variance for compatibility with GPT-2 TensorFlow weights (4.2 sidebar).
Keep qkv_bias False by default; revisit when loading OpenAI GPT-2 weights (4.1).
Call model.eval() before generation to disable dropout (4.7).
Count parameters with sum(p.numel()) and memory as params x 4 bytes for float32 (4.6).
Keep separate token-embedding and output layers for training; the author finds they train better than weight tying (4.6).
